song.title: Sing Yourself A Happy Song
song.author: Mark and Helen Johnson
song.summary: This song, in three parts, has a practical application: ‘to make the job a bit easier’. A great excuse to sing together, and huge fun.
song.teachingTips:
• This song is a great introduction to singing in harmony.
  • The different verses have some big vocal jumps in the melody. Make sure voices are warmed up properly to help sing these leaps cleanly. Begin by making a siren sound, going up high and down low. This will help warm up the vocal cords. Then, try using a warm-up like Ear Warm from S!ng Warm-ups.
  • As an introduction to pitching intervals, sing up a scale using the numbers 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8, then back down 8 7 6 5 4 3 2 1. Then try an arpeggio 1 3 5 3 1. Then try other permutations e.g. 1 2 1 3 1 4 1 5 1 6 1 7 1 8.

assembly.title: Extra Energy
assembly.description: What wakes you up in the morning? From birdsong to sprouting leaves and Easter eggs, this assembly helps us to celebrate all the energy of springtime.

assembly.title: Feeling Hopeful
assembly.description: This assembly explores the meaning of hope and what it will take to realize our ambitions for the future.

assembly.title: Feeling Awake
assembly.description: This assembly uses The Parable of the Sower to reflect on what is needed to be ‘awake and ready for action’ in school.

assembly.title: Feeling Good
assembly.description: This assembly explores the uniqueness of human beings and how we can help others to feel more valuable.

resources.title: Musical Ladders
resources.content:
[{"key":"4744ff9552234593","layout":"icon-bullet","attributes":{"body":"
  • To hear the difference between musical intervals
  • To identify, play and sing musical intervals
","title":"What’s achievable","noMargin":false,"image":"https://assets.sparkyard.com/uploads/icons/green-star-1614702483w2iKm.png"}},{"key":"e4f1aea9b8e94ff6","layout":"icon-bullet","attributes":{"body":"

Pieces of paper labelled with letter names of a C major scale; keyboards (notes C-C with stickers on) or pitched percussion (notes C-C) 

","title":"What you need","noMargin":false,"image":"https://assets.sparkyard.com/uploads/icons/blue-wrench-16147025258WedI.png"}},{"key":"7112a3384fd0d615","layout":"wysiwyg","attributes":{"body":"

The melody of this song has some big leaps in it. The musical distance (leap) from one note to another is called an interval. Try this activity to practise counting intervals and playing them to see what they sound like.

Place eight pieces of paper in a vertical line on the floor and label them: C D E F G A B C. This is your ‘musical ladder’ or scale. Ask two volunteers to stand on two of the ‘notes’. Count and sing up the steps between the two notes to fi nd the musical interval. Remember to include the start and end notes in your count (e.g. D-A would be a fifth, and E-F would be a second).

When you have identified the interval, ask the class to play it using keyboards or pitched percussion instruments such as glockenspiels, xylophones or chime bars. Can they try singing the intervals, with one person singing the bottom note and the other singing the top one? 

","title":"","noMargin":false,"background_color":null}},{"key":"31355c27db0df3a6","layout":"icon-bullet","attributes":{"body":"

Can the children think of and identify any other intervals outside of the classroom, for example a door bell, a cuckoo, a mobile phone ringtone, the first four notes of the Star Wars Theme, the call ‘yoo hoo’? Musical intervals are all around us! 

","title":"Branch Out","noMargin":false,"image":"https://assets.sparkyard.com/uploads/icons/u1874-1614695090s5QJx.png"}}]
resources.summary: Have fun learning about musical intervals with this musical-ladders activity.

Rainbow Dance <\/strong>by Len Lye (1936) is a combination of experimental film, jazz and dance and is an inspiring watch! After watching the film, encourage the children to think about what movements spring brings: plants growing; raindrops falling; children running, jumping and skipping in the playground. Then, think about the colours of spring. Create a contemporary dance piece that expresses this collision of movement and colours to showcase in one of your spring assemblies. <\/p>\n","title":"","noMargin":false,"background_color":null}},{"key":"279afe7bf7efd6b1","layout":"video","attributes":{"url":"https:\/\/www.youtube.com\/watch?v=AHN9IHGQxk8","title":"Rainbow Dance","active":false,"noMargin":false,"background_color":null}}]

resources.title: Happy Or Sad Game
resources.content:
[{"key":"281343790f419b73","layout":"wysiwyg","attributes":{"body":"

Think about how our body shape changes when we are happy and when we’re sad. Our mouths turn up when we’re happy and down when we’re sad; our heads tend to drop and our shoulders droop when we’re sad; we tend to sit up straight with our heads up when we are happy, but all hunched up when we are sad.

Try some ‘happy’ and ‘sad’ poses and get the rest of the class to guess your mood. This activity could be done with pipe-cleaner people. Ask the children to bend their ‘person’ into a happy or a sad pose.

","title":"","noMargin":false}}]

resources.title: Syncopated Rhythms
resources.content:
[{"key":"61ae53380787e273","layout":"wysiwyg","attributes":{"body":"

Ideal for a single session

","title":"","noMargin":false}},{"key":"7ec9e28599f39ca3","layout":"icon-bullet","attributes":{"body":"
  • To recognize a syncopated rhythm
  • To maintain a syncopated rhythm accurately and in time as a group
","title":"What’s achievable","noMargin":false,"image":"https://assets.sparkyard.com/uploads/icons/green-star-1614702483w2iKm.png"}},{"key":"5fb2117a34261572","layout":"icon-bullet","attributes":{"body":"

Untuned percussion instruments

","title":"What you need","noMargin":false,"image":"https://assets.sparkyard.com/uploads/icons/blue-wrench-16147025258WedI.png"}},{"key":"91c44053c43efc6f","layout":"icon-bullet","attributes":{"body":"

Syncopated; offbeat; rhythm; polyrhythmic; texture

","title":"Key vocabulary","noMargin":false,"image":"https://assets.sparkyard.com/uploads/icons/icons-keyvocab-280x280-27-1620218359Ng3ET.png"}},{"key":"de0e7b51714c2e49","layout":"wysiwyg","attributes":{"body":"

The song choices for this activity use syncopated rhythms. Explain that a syncopated rhythm is a placement of notes off the beat. However, the best way to understand syncopated rhythms is to get everyone singing them and feeling them!

To begin with, choose either Christmas Has Started or Sing Yourself A Happy Song and make sure everyone is familiar with the first two verses (and chorus for Christmas Has Started). Select lines from the song and get everyone to clap the rhythm. Is everyone able to clap the rhythm accurately?

Next, practise the syncopated rhythm of the title phrase, ‘Christmas has started’ or ‘Sing yourself a happy song’. Get everyone chanting the rhythm first, then try clapping or perhaps perform it using body percussion. 

Syncopated Rhythm – Christmas has started

","title":"","noMargin":false}},{"key":"161c9814cd4bf305","layout":"image","attributes":{"image":"https://assets.sparkyard.com/uploads/MusicCurriculum/MusicCurr-ASSETS/YEAR5/year5-musiccurr-syncopatedrhythms953-1634033034vVNUT.png","title":"","noMargin":false}},{"key":"eac3bcf3568e8ea5","layout":"wysiwyg","attributes":{"body":"

Syncopated Rhythm – Sing yourself a happy song

","title":"","noMargin":false}},{"key":"f10c27abe270f303","layout":"image","attributes":{"image":"https://assets.sparkyard.com/uploads/MusicCurriculum/MusicCurr-ASSETS/YEAR5/year5-musiccurr-syncopatedrhythms953-2-1634033034QnMo3.png","title":"","noMargin":false}},{"key":"6bc0336f411166ca","layout":"wysiwyg","attributes":{"body":"

Then, play the rhythm on untuned percussion instruments, such as claves, woodblocks or drums. Divide the group in half and get one side to sing the song while the other side plays the syncopated rhythm. This will produce a fun, polyrhythmic texture to accompany the song and will require a good deal of concentration to keep at the same tempo. Swap groups so all have a turn playing the syncopated rhythm.

","title":"","noMargin":false}},{"key":"a5663d919a3eade9","layout":"icon-bullet","attributes":{"body":"

Try singing some other songs with a syncopated rhythm in the melody. Harvest Samba, When It’s A Sunny Day, Calypso Carol, Mary’s Boy Child and ’S No Problem are all really good examples.

","title":"Branch Out","noMargin":false,"image":"https://assets.sparkyard.com/uploads/icons/u1874-1614695090s5QJx.png"}},{"key":"3ea1407415039366","layout":"title-block","attributes":{"title":"Assessment Suggestions","background_color":"#009CCF"}},{"key":"72ffcab5ec3f0fa1","layout":"wysiwyg","attributes":{"body":"
  • Can they clap syncopated rhythms accurately?
  • Can they maintain rhythms accurately and in time as a group?
","title":"","noMargin":false}}]
